newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court hears sex-predator confinement law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court hears sex-predator confinement law.

text.p: The Supreme Court debated on Tuesday whether states may confine dangerous sex offenders to mental institutions after they serve their prison sentences.

Kansas Attorney General Carla Stovall defended the state follow-up confinement laws as providing treatment to mentally ill, violent sex offenders who pose a great risk of committing more crimes if released.

But Thomas Weilert, representing a convicted, repeat child molester who challenged the law, argued that a state cannot constitutionally continue confinement once the prison sentence has been served because that amounts to permanent punishment.
"What is the state supposed to do, just wait until he goes out and does it again?" Chief Justice William Rehnquist asked.

Weilert said the state has other options available, such as restrictions on a sex offender's parole and requirements to stay away from schools or children. But Justice Sandra Day O'Connor said such requirments were "just not very effective."
During the arguments, the justices vigorously questioned both attorneys about the laws, which have been adopted in six states and illustrate a nationwide effort to crack down on child molesters.
State Attorney Stovall said civil commitment represents a new way to deal with sex offenders. Previously, the state could either impose criminal punishment or treatment instead of such punishment.
O'Connor asked if the state could simply "lock up any violent offender" with a mental abnormality of any kind if the Supreme Court upholds this law.
Stovall said the two key factors to be decided were the medical justification and the criminal's dangerousness.
She said courts historically have not considered civil commitment as punishment, and the treatment goals were much different than the purpose of retribution and deterrence in criminal sentences.
Weilert disagreed, saying the law extends confinement after the prison term has been finished and amounts to "effective permanent incarceration."
Rehnquist noted that the Kansas Supreme Court, which struck down the law, said a state as an alternative could impose a life sentence for sex offenders.

But Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said the state in the confinement law may be seeking to do "something gentler and kinder" than a life sentence. "Why does the court force the most harsh sentence?" she asked.
Justice Antonin Scalia answered for Weilert, saying the state may have to take the harshest possible punishment because it would be less open to possible manipulation.
The case involved Leroy Hendricks, 62, who has a long record of sex offences. The state had him committed to a mental facility after he served a 10-year prison term.
"It is a second incarceration for the same criminal act he committed in 1984," Weilert said.
He admitted Hendricks likely would commit more sex crimes against children if freed, but said that prediction was insufficient to keep him confined.

Rehnquist asked if the state could confine a mentally ill person who would commit murder. "We would be treading on very thin ice," Weilert said, adding that predictions of future criminal acts would not be enough.
The high court took the case under advisement, with a ruling due by the middle of next year.
